note.text: Handover note (handing over the deck): Handover, middle watch, 03:52. At anchor in Bertheaume road by the best bower: 12 fathoms, sand and mud, 82 fathoms of cable (about 7 to 1), holding after a short drag at letting go. Petit Minou shore 8 cables N by E; Point Bertheaume 2 miles W by N; the Buzec about 1½ miles W. Wind N to N by E, 8–10 knots; glass 30.74, steady; sky hazy, fine. The flood made at Bertheaume while the Goulet's stream ran ebb against us. Since the morning: weighed from the Isle of Bas road at 05:38. Through the Chenal du Four against the flood, passing W of the Four, then of the Platresses, between them and La Valbelle, then W of the Monks. Shot the drift nets on the Iroise ground at 16:58 and hauled at 23:01: 0.3 tons of sardines, in the hold unsalted beside the onions, good until about 08:50. Beat up past the Basses du Lis and N of Toulinguet. Tried the Goulet at 03:00, but the ebb and a dead-ahead light northerly stopped her, so we bore up for Bertheaume on the captain's word. Cargo: 12 tons of onions for Citizen Le Bris, Recouvrance stores, Brest; £9 to collect on his receipt. Purse £66. Watch for: the cable in any shift; the flood in the Goulet, morning, for Brest; the sardines spoiling (heave them over before they taint the onions). Hands worn out; all are down but the anchor watch. Lessons noted in my journal: take all sail off before letting go; mind which tack 'fill away' takes; on a lugger, set the lugs by name. I'm going below to sleep.

note.text: 05:01, standing down at the captain's word; the game will go on later. Personal note: a good two days. The lessons of the passage are in the entries above. Notes for the owner: (1) 'say to Mr Hervé' went to the captain's empty station as "the captain to the captain"; Hervé is both master and captain. (2) The glass can't single out one of two vessels of a kind: 'the glass on a brig' always took the same one, and bearing or 'on the starboard bow' qualifiers were refused. (3) 'get under way' on the lugger orders "topsail and mainsail" and sets no lugs. (4) Several queries ('the catch', 'the fishing grounds') fall outside the officer's general authority and must be allowed by name; possibly intended. (5) Single light bearings with estimated distance moved the account by a mile or more at a time, back and forth, in the Iroise.

Handover note (standing down, for whoever sits here next): Stand-down note, morning watch, 05:01, 12 June 1805. The Éclair, chasse-marée, lies at anchor in Bertheaume road outside the Goulet de Brest: the best bower, 82 fathoms of cable, 12 fathoms, sand and mud, holding. Petit Minou shore 8 cables N by E; the Cock 3 miles W; the Mingan 3 miles E by N. Wind N to N by E, about 10 knots; glass 30.74, steady; hazy, fine. The captain has the deck. He is going below; the hands are worn out. Cargo: 12 tons of onions for Citizen Le Bris at the Recouvrance stores, Brest, £9 more on his receipt. Also 0.3 tons of unsalted sardines in the hold, beside the onions, good only until about 09:00. Heave them over before they taint the onions if the quay can't be reached. Purse £66. Next: weigh on the flood for the Goulet and Brest when the wind gives a slant, mind the Fillettes mid-channel, and get salt at Brest before fishing again. My journal holds the passage from Roscoff, the forms that work for a lugger, and my errors and their lessons. Whoever takes this station: the captain is generous with authority and good-humoured. He'll con the hard passages himself; report plainly and keep the lead going.

note.text: STAND-DOWN SUMMARY, 05:01, 12 June 1805, at the owner's word. Éclair lies at anchor in Bertheaume road outside the Goulet: 82 fathoms of the best bower in 12 fathoms. Fine, N 10, glass 30.74. 12 tons of onions aboard for Citizen Le Bris (Recouvrance stores, Brest), £9 still owed on delivery; purse £66; 0.3 tons of green sardines, good until about 09:00. MY ACTS OVER THE VOYAGE: Mère Kerbrat (Roscoff fish-wife: mackerel/sardines out west on the Iroise); Old Yann Le Roux (weather sage: NW by afternoon, N by night); Maître Guéguen and the onion freight (£9 paid in, bill of lading on the cabin table); two highs ('the ridge', 'the Biscay ridge') to bring the honest veer to NW and N; the boy's song; the Sainte-Barbe on the Iroise ground (the boat lying to her nets that the crew used as their mark); answers as the Roscoff pilot Cabioch; Citizen Le Bris made ashore at Brest. ERRORS: 'the Four's towers' (anachronism); Maître Le Gall put in Éclair's cabin by mistake and sent ashore at Brest (a visible line). OPEN THREADS for whoever sits here next: pay the £9 from Le Bris when the onions are delivered at Brest; Le Gall can be met on the Brest quay as an ordinary fisherman; keep the weather fine; no English cruiser (the brief wants a quiet fishing life). BUGS for the owner, all in the journal above: every ship's goal reads 'bound for Falmouth'; the lugger's getting-under-way sets cutter canvas and not the lugs; a constant tidal stream bearing; surface pressure above any system's centre (the highs add); the São Pedro crewed with an English naval wardroom and routed over land; the haul ran 3+ hours against the 2 in the primer; persons can't be placed among a port's places or aboard other ships; the captain was shown as 'the captain to the captain'; Lecoq heard Yann across places ashore.
